report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) transforms what we know about the world into intelligent, adaptive behaviour.
Existing theories have traditionally explained this function through cross-circuit interactions, where PFC neurons control sensory-action mappings elsewhere in the brain.
However, recent findings reveal a remarkable organisation of neuronal activity that enables flexible computation within the PFC itself.

These findings motivate a framework of duplicated and structured representations (DSRs), where the abstract structure of the world is embedded locally in connections between prefrontal neurons encoding conjunctions of action and context.
We review an extensive body of empirical findings showing that DSRs explain canonical PFCdependent behaviours as diverse as sequence working memory, planning, and value-guided decisions.
In each case, PFC neurons represent multiple actions simultaneously.
Structured connectivity between these action representations then guides local network dynamics to infer how behaviour should be organised -simplifying both computation and readout.
Taken further, the same logic offers a mechanistic foothold on some of the PFC's most elusive functions, including hierarchical reasoning and social computations.
Overall, the DSR framework provides a unified understanding of prefrontal computations and a tractable basis for a new generation of mechanistic research.
How can we make sense of these seemingly disparate roles of PFC, from gating simple stimulus-response mappings to sequential planning, schematic inferences, and social computations?
Cognitive neuroscience has made great strides towards uncovering the computational principles used by the PFC to achieve behavioural flexibility.

A dominant view has emerged, which proposes that the PFC encodes the abstract contexts governing behaviour -the "if-then" conditionals that make Hassan prioritise weeding over watering after a rainy night.
Under this regime, structured knowledge is encoded by abstract prefrontal context representations that are dissociated, or "factorised", from representations of concrete actions and sensory inputs (
Our rich repertoire of behaviours, and ability to adjust them when necessary, is central to our success in a changing world (Miller et al., 1960).
text.formatted: Our rich repertoire of behaviours, and ability to adjust them when necessary, is central to our success in a changing world <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Miller et al., 1960)</ref>.

text.text: This flexibility requires us to turn knowledge about the world into organised actions that serve our current goals, a process that critically involves the Prefrontal cortex (PFC; see Supplementary Box 1 for a discussion of PFC definitions).
Indeed, PFC damage often spares knowledge of the world while impairing the ability to use it to guide behaviour (Duncan et al., 1996; Shallice, 1982; Shallice and Burgess, 1991).
text.formatted: Indeed, PFC damage often spares knowledge of the world while impairing the ability to use it to guide behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Duncan et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Shallice, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Shallice and Burgess, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the dramatic expansion of the primate PFC has been linked to our unique capacity to devise new ways of organising complex behaviours (Klein-Flügge et al., 2022; Passingham, 2021), such as those that enabled the invention of farming in ancient Mesopotamia (Smith, 1995; Zeder, 2011).
text.formatted: Moreover, the dramatic expansion of the primate PFC has been linked to our unique capacity to devise new ways of organising complex behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Klein-Flügge et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Passingham, 2021)</ref>, such as those that enabled the invention of farming in ancient Mesopotamia <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Smith, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Zeder, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Such a revolutionary invention necessitated inferring how our actions, and those of others, would change under a multitude of different scenarios -like changing weather conditions, market demands and family dynamics.
The PFC is strongly implicated in such inferences about ourselves and others (Klein-Flügge et al., 2022; Mahmoodi and Rushworth, 2026).
text.formatted: The PFC is strongly implicated in such inferences about ourselves and others <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Klein-Flügge et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Mahmoodi and Rushworth, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Yet this diversity of functions poses a challenge for any attempt at a unified mechanistic understanding.
An emerging body of work suggests an additional type of representation that coexists with factorised representations of abstract context.
These findings reveal that the PFC itself computes possible actions through two key representational features.

First, dedicated neurons explicitly represent possible actions, and these representations are duplicated across different contexts -different neurons represent the same action depending on its context.

Second, structured knowledge is embedded in the connectivity between these duplicated representations, allowing knowledge about the outside world or internal states to shape which combinations of actions can be encoded.

Together, duplication and structured connectivity allow the PFC to encode "local copies" of possible actions whose organisation is constrained by synaptic connectivity that embeds abstract structure (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: Together, duplication and structured connectivity allow the PFC to encode "local copies" of possible actions whose organisation is constrained by synaptic connectivity that embeds abstract structure (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: These two features therefore allow the PFC itself to compute over possible actions -it no longer acts merely as a mediator between stimulus and response in other circuits.
Instead, the burden of behavioural control is shifted inwards, to local network dynamics within the PFC.
In this review, we highlight a growing body of empirical findings that can be understood through this framework of duplicated and structured representations (DSRs) in the PFC.
We first explain the representation and its algorithmic implications.

We then outline how it provides a mechanistic framework that explains emerging empirical data across diverse PFC-dependent tasks, from stimulus-response mappings through value learning to sequence working memory and planning.

Finally, we discuss how DSRs align with the diverse functions of different PFC subregions, shedding new light on the evolutionary expansion of PFC and its role in hierarchical reasoning and social inference.
For simplicity, we visually illustrate DSRs using single neurons tuned to conjunctions of actions and contexts.
However, the same computational principles apply when such conjunctions are encoded at the population level (Supplementary Box 2).
How does the PFC translate abstract knowledge into flexible behaviour?
Consider Hassan, an experienced farmer on the modern-day Euphrates who reorganises his actions depending on the weather.
In dry conditions he fertilizes before sowing, but plants first if rain is expected (Figure 1c).
text.formatted: In dry conditions he fertilizes before sowing, but plants first if rain is expected (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>).

text.text: Crucially, he can also imagine how his actions, and those of others, would change if the world was different.
When his daughter finally gets the tractor she has always dreamed of, Hassan will immediately know how this will reshape both their daily schedules.

A wealth of evidence places the PFC at the top of an action selection hierarchy critical for mediating such complex inferences (Fine and Hayden, 2021; Fuster, 2000; Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007; Miller et al., 1960).
text.formatted: A wealth of evidence places the PFC at the top of an action selection hierarchy critical for mediating such complex inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Fine and Hayden, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Fuster, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Koechlin and Summerfield, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Miller et al., 1960)</ref>.

text.text: Here, actions encompass a broad set of volitional choices about states that can be planned over, from concrete limb movements to more abstract decisions like navigating to a particular goal.
Under this view, PFC neurons represent possible ways of actively organising future actions rather than passively predicting sensory outcomes (Fine and Hayden, 2021; Miller et al., 1960).
text.formatted: Under this view, PFC neurons represent possible ways of actively organising future actions rather than passively predicting sensory outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Fine and Hayden, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Miller et al., 1960)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that this function depends critically on a pervasive representational principle.
The activity of PFC neurons explicitly represents possible actions, and their connectivity embeds structured knowledge that organises these actions.
These representations have two key features.
They are: 1-Duplicated: The PFC uses different neurons, or different population activity patterns (Supplementary Box 2), to represent the same action depending on its context.
For example, representations can be duplicated for different ordinal positions; different expected times; different levels of preference; or different task rules.
In sequential behaviours, representations are duplicated according to ordinal position.
Different populations in Hassan's PFC represent the same 'sowing' action depending on whether it is planned for today, tomorrow, or the day after (Figure 1c).
text.formatted: Different populations in Hassan's PFC represent the same 'sowing' action depending on whether it is planned for today, tomorrow, or the day after (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>).

text.text: When actions are ranked by preference, representations of the same action are instead duplicated according to their rank.
The same plan to 'plant rice' is represented by different neurons depending on whether it is the first, second, or third priority (Figure 1d).
text.formatted: The same plan to 'plant rice' is represented by different neurons depending on whether it is the first, second, or third priority (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1d</ref>).

text.text: Action representations can also be duplicated according to the sensorimotor mappings specified by different 'rules'.
For example, one set of neurons might encode that "Hassan should water tomorrow if it is dry", while another would encode that "Hassan should water tomorrow if his niece comes over to help".
Crucially, such tuning generalises across different action combinations -the same neurons encode a particular conjunction of action and context regardless of which actions occur in other contexts.
For example, a neuron encoding 'plant oats at position 2' fires whenever this action occupies that position, regardless of which actions fill the remaining positions (Figure 1d).
text.formatted: For example, a neuron encoding 'plant oats at position 2' fires whenever this action occupies that position, regardless of which actions fill the remaining positions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1d</ref>).

text.text: DSRs are therefore 'combinatorial': new combinations -or "assemblies" -of neurons within the local network can represent any of the many possible action combinations, including hypothetical ones that have never been executed before.
The result is a highly expressive network brimming with possibilities.
2-Structured: Our actions are structured by knowledge of the world and ourselves.
This knowledge renders some action combinations more probable than others.
Such 'action statistics' can reflect the structure of a particular environment, mirror the abstract rules of a particular task, or emerge from internally generated constraints.
We propose that the vast combinatorial landscape of duplicated representations is sculpted by the statistical relationships between actions.
For instance, knowledge of seasonal food preferences will constrain connectivity between crop representations in Hassan's PFC to determine the order of his planting cycles.
In other words, action statistics should constrain the connectivity between the local action copies.
Neurons encoding more probable ways of organising actions excite each other, and those encoding improbable action patterns are mutually inhibitory.
When this connectivity is persistently active (Box 1), it stabilises neuronal assemblies representing highly probable action combinations (Figure 1e).
text.formatted: When this connectivity is persistently active (Box 1), it stabilises neuronal assemblies representing highly probable action combinations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1e</ref>).

text.text: These assemblies become "attractor" states of the network dynamics, which are more likely to be expressed in the network than assemblies representing alternative action combinations (Figure 1e).
text.formatted: These assemblies become "attractor" states of the network dynamics, which are more likely to be expressed in the network than assemblies representing alternative action combinations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1e</ref>).

text.text: Structured connectivity can also be gated (Box 1).
In this case, it only mediates information transfer after a control signal is received.
This could be an external stimulus, but it could also reflect internal signals indicating execution of an action or a change in internal state.
Such gated connectivity allows the PFC to perform various operations over duplicated representations (Figure 1f).

text.text: Crucially, structured connectivity between duplicated representations does not need to be monosynaptic.

Multi-synaptic pathways can impose equivalent structural constraints on action representations. stabilise representations of more likely action combinations. The relative timing of neuronal activity is critical to represent an action sequence.

Timing information is not needed to represent the sequence. (h) DSRs enable compositional generalisation and a linear readout without the need for exponentially many neurons.
It does, however, use more neurons than the factorised solution -especially as the number of actions (A) and contexts (N) increases.
Duplicated and structured representations (DSRs) allow the PFC to organise behaviours through local dynamics.
Dedicated neurons are tuned to different possible actions, and the relationships between actions are constrained by the network connectivity.
This allows recurrent network dynamics to translate structured knowledge into flexible processing of complex, multi-action behaviours.
Under DSRs, the PFC represents several relevant actions simultaneously in the activity of different neuronal populations.
Multiple actions can now be processed concurrently -an idea postulated by Lashley as early as the 1950s (Lashley, 1951).
text.formatted: Multiple actions can now be processed concurrently -an idea postulated by Lashley as early as the 1950s <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Lashley, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: The challenge of organising actions, such as forming extended plans, is reduced to simply selecting among different assemblies within the local network.
DSRs therefore differ from factorised representations, where the organisation of actions is encoded in the temporal pattern of neuronal activity (Figure 1g).
text.formatted: DSRs therefore differ from factorised representations, where the organisation of actions is encoded in the temporal pattern of neuronal activity (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1g</ref>).

text.text: A prominent example of this temporal coding is hippocampal replay, where several place cells fire one after another to encode a sequence of locations (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996).
text.formatted: A prominent example of this temporal coding is hippocampal replay, where several place cells fire one after another to encode a sequence of locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: In this case, the encoded action sequence can only be deciphered by integrating information over time, which is substantially more complicated than reading static assemblies (Branco et al., 2010; Buzsáki, 2010).
text.formatted: In this case, the encoded action sequence can only be deciphered by integrating information over time, which is substantially more complicated than reading static assemblies <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Branco et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Buzsáki, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: By representing action combinations with static assemblies, duplication facilitates efficient "linear" readout by other sensory, motor, and memory systems.
This simplified neural readout is similar in spirit to that offered by random non-linear mixed selectivity described in the PFC and wider neocortex (Rigotti et al., 2013; Tye et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This simplified neural readout is similar in spirit to that offered by random non-linear mixed selectivity described in the PFC and wider neocortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Rigotti et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Tye et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Both theories rely on high-dimensional representations to simplify downstream readout of conjunctive information, like actions and their contexts.
However, they also have important differences.
First, the duplication in DSRs is a special case of non-linear mixed selectivity, where the tuning of neurons to conjunctions of actions and contexts generalises across different action combinations.
This enables flexible combinatorial coding of new action combinations (Figure 1c,d).
text.formatted: This enables flexible combinatorial coding of new action combinations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>,<ref type="figure">d</ref>).

text.text: Second, DSRs are not random projections of actions and contexts.
Instead, they are connected in a way that embeds structured knowledge about the world (Figure 1b,e,f).
text.formatted: Instead, they are connected in a way that embeds structured knowledge about the world (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>,<ref type="figure">e</ref>,<ref type="figure">f</ref>).

text.text: This not only enables efficient readout, but also allows powerful computations over future actions within the local PFC network.
DSRs are poised for efficient computation.
Inference happens locally through simple attractor dynamics that are constrained by the structure of the world and internal goals.
By pre-configuring such structure into connectivity between action copies, network activity is steered towards stable assemblies that encode action sequences.
Under DSRs, planning therefore becomes equivalent to recognition.

Just as visual cortical activity is shaped by the statistics of visual scenes (Iacaruso et al., 2017; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Marr, 2010) (Box 1), we propose that PFC activity is shaped by the statistical patterns of action transitions.
text.formatted: Just as visual cortical activity is shaped by the statistics of visual scenes <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Iacaruso et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Lee and Nguyen, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Marr, 2010)</ref> (Box 1), we propose that PFC activity is shaped by the statistical patterns of action transitions.

text.text: This allows inference of future actions instead of objects and minimises the need for costly sequential planning at decision time.
DSRs therefore unify our understanding of the PFC with other cortical regions that embed statistical structure in synaptic connections to enable efficient neural computation (Marr, 2010).
text.formatted: DSRs therefore unify our understanding of the PFC with other cortical regions that embed statistical structure in synaptic connections to enable efficient neural computation <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Marr, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, when this structured connectivity is gated, it enables abstract operations over multiple actions.
Swaps, reversals and comparisons can now be computed locally, simultaneously, and on demand.
Together, these features endow DSRs with remarkable flexibility and efficiency in organising our actions to solve new problems.
At the core of this efficiency is the combinatorial nature of DSR duplication.
This is distinct from the "cloning" in clone-structured cognitive graphs (CSCGs; George et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is distinct from the "cloning" in clone-structured cognitive graphs (CSCGs; <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">George et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas CSCG states are split based on sequential history to de-alias similar observations, DSR actions are systematically copied across contexts to span all possible action combinations.

Notably, the rich de-aliased representations built by CSCGs, such as place cells, can themselves serve as inputs to DSR duplication in the PFC, building a combinatorial code of possible future locations (e.g. see Section 3.1.2).
DSRs are computationally efficient, but this efficiency requires large neuronal populations.
To encode all possible action combinations, every conjunction of action (A) and context (N) must be represented by a different pattern of neural activity.

This differs from the 'factorised' representations proposed in the switchboard view of the PFC, where actions and contexts are encoded in separate neurons and combined via gating or synaptic plasticity at decision time (Behrens et al., 2018; Burgess and Hitch, 1999; Eichenbaum, 2004; Whittington et al., 2020) (Figure 1a,g,h).

text.text: However, this neuronal cost of DSRs is justified for two reasons.
First, DSRs are more computationally flexible and efficient than factorised solutions (Section 2.2.1,2.2.2).
Second, DSRs can be more neuronally efficient than alternative solutions that encode each combination of actions in a different neuron.
This depends on how much flexibility is needed (Dorrell et al., 2026).

text.text: If Hassan always plants his crops in the same order, a single neuron suffices to encode this stereotyped "planting" sequence.
If he instead wants to consider all possible sequences, assigning one neuron per sequence uses more neurons (A N ) than the combinatorial DSR regime (Figure 1h).

text.text: To summarise, we propose that the PFC leverages large neuronal resources to build expressive representations that allow efficient readout and inference.

By duplicating action representations across different contexts and then connecting these duplicates to reflect structured action statistics, DSRs allow generalisation and efficient inference across a broad swathe of different behaviours.
We next explore a growing body of empirical findings that can be understood through DSRs.
Recent decades have seen a surge in high-yield neurophysiological data (Jun et al., 2017; Pachitariu et al., 2016; Zong et al., 2022) obtained during increasingly more sophisticated tasks.

text.text: These advances have revealed rich representations and dynamics within the PFC itself that go far beyond simple contextual gating of activity in other brain regions.
In this section, we show that the DSR framework provides a unifying lens for understanding such rich PFC data across paradigms.
We start with sequential tasks that range from simple sequence working memory to complex planning.
We then consider tasks where actions are organised by stimulus-response rules or ranked by preference.
Across these paradigms, DSRs provide a framework that explains how neuronal dynamics can implement canonical PFC-dependent computations.
We begin with action sequences.

text.text: Thanks to improved neuronal recordings, the field has made substantial strides in understanding the underlying neural computations.
One way to generate a sequence is to simply retrieve it.
In such sequence working memory (SWM) tasks, subjects hold a cued chain of actions in memory and execute it in the correct order after a short delay.
The DSR framework suggests that different actions are represented by different neurons depending on their relative order in the sequence.

Consistent with this idea, early studies in macaques performing SWM tasks described frontal neurons tuned to conjunctions of action and ordinal position (Barone and Joseph, 1989; Botvinick and Watanabe, 2007; Funahashi et al., 1997; Inoue and Mikami, 2006; Ninokura et al., 2004 Ninokura et al., , 2003;; Rigotti et al., 2013; Tanji, 2001).

text.text: Intriguingly, this principle can also extend to inference of action sequences.

Action representations are duplicated according to ordinal position, and gated connections map action representations from the "next" position to the "now" position, and from "next + 1" to "next", etc. (e) DSRs predict that, at execution time, conveyor belt dynamics read out the sequence one element at a time.

As an action is executed, the remaining action representations are shifted by one position: a new action is moved to the "now" position then executed, leading to a further shift along the conveyor belt.
The same duplicated representations that support SWM can, when their connectivity embeds knowledge of the world, do more than retrieve sequences from memory.
They can infer new ones.

We plan in rich ways by leveraging our internal world model to generate new action sequences.

text.text: In section 3.1.2, we saw that connecting duplicated representations of the same action at different ordinal positions supports simple inferences like loop closure.
However, DSRs can also generalise structured connectivity to enable richer inferences.
This requires structured information to be embedded in connections between duplicated representations of different actions across ordinal positions.
Such connectivity should follow a simple principle: neurons are mutually excitatory if they represent compatible actions, and mutually inhibitory if they do not.

For example, if Hassan has to avoid manual labor on the farm after a surgery, the representation of a scheduled surgery tomorrow should inhibit the representation of harvesting the day after (Figure 4a).

text.text: The resulting 'spacetime attractor' network steers representations towards plausible action sequences conditioned on a distant goal.

Planning takes the form of attractor dynamics that simultaneously refine the plan backwards from the goal and forwards from the current state to converge on an entire action sequence, which can then be executed through the conveyorbelt mechanism discussed before (Botvinick and Plaut, 2006; El-Gaby et al., 2024; Jensen et al., 2026; Whittington et al., 2025).

text.text: This contrasts with common planning algorithms that use sequential search to evaluate actions one by one.

This distinction can be resolved in fMRI by testing whether representations are conjunctive for action and ordinal position, as DSRs predict, or encode action alone, as sequential rollout would predict.
Finally, DSRs propose that plans can be computed by prefrontal attractor dynamics.

It would also naturally arise if plans were inferred within a DSR itself, where representations gradually propagate away from both the current location and distant goals to infer intermediate actions.
Together, these results suggest that duplicated representations extend from working memory to internally generated action plans.

DSRs simplify such 'computations over sequences' because the entire future is represented concurrently, which facilitates simultaneous operations over multiple actions.

text.text: It also reveals remarkable flexibility in PFC representations, where information can be moved between different ordinal positions depending on control signals from the environment.
Dedicated temporary subspaces allow common transformations, like reversals, to be carried out efficiently without the need to re-infer the updated sequence de novo.
Other abstract operations can similarly be implemented through such 'gated' subspaces that conjunctively code for an operation and the variables it operates over.
These flexible operations over concurrent representations bear a striking resemblance to the transformer architecture that has revolutionised machine learning.
Transformers represent extended sequences concurrently, which allows an 'attention mechanism' to integrate information across time (Vaswani et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Transformers represent extended sequences concurrently, which allows an 'attention mechanism' to integrate information across time <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Vaswani et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This approach outperforms previous methods that process sequence elements one by one.
The PFC may have arrived at the same solution: parallelising representations to enable powerful inferences and abstract operations through network dynamics.
We now turn to prefrontal computations in non-sequential settings.

Under DSRs, flexible processing of parallel action representations provides insights into a wide range of PFC-dependent contextual behaviours that require comparisons and integration of information about multiple possible actions.
What unites these behaviours is a common principle: structured knowledge is used to organise actions flexibly when demands change.
We highlight two especially prominent cases, where actions are either organised by the rules that govern them or by their changing priorities.
A hallmark of PFC-dependent flexibility is the ability to switch between different stimulus-response mappings depending on the context.
In such 'set-shifting' tasks, identical stimuli call for different actions depending on which 'rule' is currently active (Birrell and Brown, 2000; Broschard et al., 2021).

text.text: This can be achieved by duplicating representations, such that the same action is represented by different neurons for different rules.
In a seminal study, Panichello and Buschman (2021) first presented monkeys with two colour cues positioned at the top and bottom of a screen (Panichello and Buschman, 2021).

Under DSRs, rule information selectively gates connections that move colour information from the appropriate input subspace into the choice subspace (Figure 5c).

text.text: Together, these results provide cross-species evidence for rule-dependent duplication of actions.
DSRs also suggest structured connectivity between the rule subspaces, which could be used to infer actions that are not explicitly cued.
Structured connectivity could impose specific dependencies between available choices: e.g. if the top colour is red, the bottom colour cannot be blue.
The same inferential machinery used for sequential behaviour in Section 3.1 could therefore operate over 'rule subspaces' to infer actions that were never explicitly cued.
Our environment is constantly changing.
To adapt, we must continually reassess which actions are most valuable.
The importance of the PFC for this flexibility is evidenced by its well-established role in reversal learning tasks (Dias et al., 1996).

text.text: In this view, the PFC meta-learns the abstract task structure through slow synaptic plasticity across many tasks.
Once learned, this structure allows rapid adaptation to structurally similar tasks via recurrent dynamics rather than further synaptic change.
Such 'learning through dynamics' echoes a key hallmark of DSRs, where connections between action copies embed the task structure to support rapid inference in new tasks via neural dynamics.
Consistent with this idea, recent theoretical work shows that neural networks can implement meta-RL by duplicating action representations according to their preference (Warren et al., 2026).

text.text: In recurrent neural networks trained on multi-armed bandit tasks with drifting rewards, duplicated representations emerged for each action.
One subspace encoded the identity of the preferred action, an orthogonal subspace encoded the second-best action, and so on (Figure 5d).

text.text: Learning in a new task then involves reorganising the appropriate actions across these rank subspaces.
Crucially, this reordering is governed by a separate representation of the value of each rank, independent of action identity.
For example, when the value of the second option exceeds the preferred option, a gated connection is activated to swap the corresponding action representations (Figure 5d).

text.text: DSRs may also encode structured dependencies between action preferences.
For example, planting may consistently have low priority whenever irrigation has high priority.
Such correlations could be embedded in persistent connectivity between representations of actions at different ranks.
This would allow inference of action preferences in an analogous way to how structured connectivity inferred action sequences in Section 3.1.2.
The DSR-based account of reward-driven learning makes three main predictions.
First, PFC neurons should duplicate action representations according to their preference.
Consistent with this, Li et al. recorded from the lateral PFC of macaques solving an economic decision-making task (Li et al., 2026).

text.text: Subjects were first shown the identity and then value of option 1, and then the identity and value of option 2.
Before 'value 2' was shown, the representations of option 1 and option 2 were orthogonal.
However, once value 2 was presented, a consistent subspace encoded the preferred option (Figure 5e).

text.text: Prefrontal representations were therefore duplicated by preference when subjects had the information necessary to rank the options.
A related literature has described non-linear mixed selectivity for actions and value in the PFC (Abe and Lee, 2011; Hayden and Platt, 2010; Johnston et al., 2024).

text.text: Within a DSR framework, such mixed selectivity arises because value correlates with rank, and different subspaces represent actions at different ranks.
Second, the PFC should encode the value associated with each rank independently of the corresponding action identity.

This idea is consistent with the widely reported finding that the PFC separately represents the value of "chosen" (preferred) and "unchosen" (non-preferred) options in binary decision tasks (Boorman et al., 2011 (Boorman et al., , 2009;; Daw et al., 2006; Fouragnan et al., 2019; Hayden et al., 2009; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008, 2006), and the value of all ranks in tasks with three options (Boorman et al., 2011; Knudsen and Wallis, 2021; Zhang et al., 2026) (Figure 5f).

text.text: Overall, the DSR framework offers a mechanistic account that could unify previously separate literatures on canonical PFC-dependent behaviours such as sequence working memory, planning, set-shifting and value-based decision making.
In all of these behaviours, PFC recordings reveal duplication of action representations across ordinal position, rule or rank.
Functional connectivity between these action duplicates embeds both concrete and abstract structures -allowing not only memory retrieval but also inferences and flexible computations over actions.
In the following section, we move beyond the classically well-studied PFC-dependent behaviours to explore how DSRs may help us understand broader, more complex roles of the PFC.
So far, we have reviewed a large literature spanning normative theories (section 2) and neural data (section 3).

To bridge the theory-data divide, the field has looked to a well-established tradition of modelling the PFC with recurrent neural networks (RNNs; Botvinick and Plaut, 2006; Wang et al., 2018; Whittington et al., 2025; Zipser et al., 1993).

text.text: However, there is an elephant in the room.
While RNNs typically use tens to hundreds of units, the human PFC boasts billions of neurons, organised into a rich landscape of anatomical and functional gradients (Passingham, 2021) (Figure 6a).

text.text: This ten-million-fold disparity suggests an intriguing possibility: perhaps the core principle motivating DSRs -trading neuronal resources for computational efficiency -extends further.
An expanded PFC could allow dedicated neuronal resources to be allocated to behaviours with distinct transition statistics, achieving efficiency not only within tasks but also across them.
Over his lifetime, Hassan will engage in a wide range of behaviours that entail distinct actions governed by unique statistics.
His hand movements when operating the tractor have different statistics to his spatial movements across the field, and both differ from his negotiations with the cattle merchant.
If you challenge a small network with enough different tasks, it will eventually reconfigure the same neurons and synapses to encode new actions and their transition statistics (Jensen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: If you challenge a small network with enough different tasks, it will eventually reconfigure the same neurons and synapses to encode new actions and their transition statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Jensen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: With a billion neurons, the PFC can afford to do something different.
It can allocate dedicated neural real estate to each class of behaviour, with connectivity tailored to its unique statistics.
This minimizes the need for synaptic plasticity when switching between different types of behaviour.
It also allows the PFC to process multiple action types in parallel, and to integrate information across these processes.
We now explore how this perspective bears on representational heterogeneity in the PFCspanning different action modalities, levels of abstraction, and even different agents.
We end by discussing how these different action statistics may emerge, through both evolution and experience.
We have known since the 1970s that different subdivisions of the PFC process different actions in line with their anatomical inputs and outputs (Goldman and Nauta, 1977; Goldman-Rakic, 1984).

text.text: These results suggest a basic idea: PFC subregions contain duplicated representations of the action modality they process.
Under the DSR framework, such duplicated representations should be connected according to the statistics of the relevant modality.
This may shed new light on action domains where mechanistic understanding remains limited, such as speech production in the inferior frontal gyrus.

text.text: If such hierarchical representations are combined with DSRs, exciting new computational possibilities emerge.
A series of DSRs at different levels of abstraction could implement hierarchical planning -a hallmark of human behaviour (Eckstein and Collins, 2020).

text.text: Critically, the use of different DSRs enables simultaneous planning across multiple levels of abstraction.
This allows the different DSRs to interact, such that actions at one level of abstraction can constrain those at another.
For example, an abstract 'task-level' DSR might infer that Hassan should harvest before his surgery.
This abstract plan could in turn constrain activity in an intermediate DSR that infers the need to refuel the tractor before beginning the harvest.
Finally, a low-level DSR would infer the path to the petrol station (Jensen et al., 2026) (Figure 6c).
text.formatted: Finally, a low-level DSR would infer the path to the petrol station <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Jensen et al., 2026)</ref> (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">6c</ref>).

text.text: This suggests a role for structured connections not just within one level of abstraction, but also across levels.
Although these additional levels of abstraction require more investment of neural resources, they enable planning over long time horizons with fewer neurons than non-hierarchical alternatives.
Instead of resource-intensive duplication of low-level actions throughout an entire plan, the distant future is represented only at a high level of abstraction.
Plans can therefore unfold efficiently, with transitions between higher levels defining higher goals and lower levels filling in the details.

Encoding the statistics of interactions in synaptic connectivity between DSRs for self and other would allow inference of their combined future.
For example, if Hassan cooks a big breakfast, his daughter will be more energized to help on the farm.

Hassan's PFC could therefore contain a system of two DSRs that jointly settle into a representation of their mutually constrained future actions, akin to planning dynamics in a single DSR (Jensen et al., 2026) (Figure 6d).

text.text: It is an intriguing prospect that such complex social interactions may become mechanistically tractable if we combine DSRs with known social specialisations across PFC subregions.

When functional specialisation in the PFC is combined with DSRs, domain-specific knowledge can be embedded in the synaptic connectivity of each PFC subregion to reflect the statistics of different actions.
These preconfigured circuits allow network dynamics to rapidly infer actions at decision time, without the need for further plasticity.
The burden of plasticity is instead shifted back to a time where the circuits are sculpted.
How and when this happens remains unclear.

On the one hand, functional subdivisions suggest the possibility of region-specific connectivity that is genetically hardwired into the circuits, similar to the hardwired encoding of attractor networks for navigation (Guardamagna et al., 2026).

text.text: This would reflect evolutionary constraints on domain-specific action statistics.
For example, to process sequences, the dlPFC might benefit from hardwired connections that link representations of the same action across adjacent ordinal positions.
This would implement conveyor belt dynamics that can recall and generate behavioural sequences (Section 3.1).
Indeed, monkeys passively viewing images had semiorthogonal dlPFC subspaces for current and past images despite not solving an explicit task (Bellet et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2024).

Learning must also play a part, to encode structures our ancestors never encountered.

CLS theory posits that this transfer happens slowly after repeated experience of a particular environment (McClelland et al., 1995).

text.text: Hassan's PFC will have DSRs for farming while chess DSRs in a professional chess player's PFC will allow faster inference in a timepressured game.

Future studies that track and manipulate activity in early postnatal development and during adult learning could help characterise both preconfigured structure and experience-dependent learning mechanisms.
Overall, extending the logic of DSRs places our mechanistic understanding within the broader context of the rich and extensive anatomy of the PFC.

Dedicating different patches of PFC to different action modalities, levels of abstraction and agents may allow embedding modality, level and agent-specific structure -allowing complex and parallel computations across different action types.
This in turn has implications for how structured representations in the PFC may emerge during development or learning.
How do we translate structured knowledge into adaptive behaviour?

Classical work has focused on factorised representations, where abstract knowledge and concrete actions are encoded by separate circuits and flexibly combined at decision time (Behrens et al., 2018; Burgess and Hitch, 1999; Eichenbaum, 2017; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Whittington et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Classical work has focused on factorised representations, where abstract knowledge and concrete actions are encoded by separate circuits and flexibly combined at decision time <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Behrens et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Burgess and Hitch, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Eichenbaum, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Miller and Cohen, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Whittington et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We have reviewed a growing literature that highlights an alternative strategy, where abstract knowledge and concrete actions are represented conjunctively in the same PFC neurons.
This shifts some of the computational burden to local circuits, emphasising the role of internal prefrontal dynamics in flexibly structuring our actions.
The result is a representational regime with all the flexibility offered by world models but with computational speed and efficiency rivalling habitual mechanisms.
DSRs in the PFC might therefore mark proficiency, reflecting an investment of neural resources to translate knowledge into efficient behaviour in domains relevant to the individual.
The DSR framework motivates future analyses of structure between local action representations.
However, elucidating structure in the PFC is challenging not only because of its size, but also because function is not easily mapped onto neuron identity.
This is in stark contrast to simpler circuits like the fruit fly brain, where it suffices to build a connectome of a single brain to map the structured connectivity between known representations.
Instead, we need to simultaneously measure prefrontal representations and connectivity de novo in each individual animal.
Proxy measures of structure based on offline neuronal coactivity can allow progress (El-Gaby et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Proxy measures of structure based on offline neuronal coactivity can allow progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(El-Gaby et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Excitingly, more direct measures of structure are also becoming feasible.

It is now possible to measure both representations and connectivity in the same neurons with optical holography (Yang and Yuste, 2018), and these tools can even be combined with freely moving neuronal imaging (Zong et al., 2022).
text.formatted: It is now possible to measure both representations and connectivity in the same neurons with optical holography <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Yang and Yuste, 2018)</ref>, and these tools can even be combined with freely moving neuronal imaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">(Zong et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These technologies may uncover how local connectivity implements flexible computations in a heterogeneous circuit like the PFC.

An important future direction will be to situate prefrontal DSRs within the broader literature on "cognitive maps", which finds structured knowledge representations throughout the brain (Behrens et al., 2018; Eichenbaum, 2004; Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).

text.text: A defining feature of DSRs is that they encode structured knowledge in a highly actionable form.
Because such knowledge is embedded into connections between action representations, it constrains efficient local computations over actions.
This avoids the more expensive cross-circuit control and online search used by other representations (Section 2).
It may also explain why PFC lesions spare semantic knowledge while disrupting the flexible organisation of behaviour it supports (Duncan et al., 1996; Shallice, 1982; Shallice and Burgess, 1991).
text.formatted: It may also explain why PFC lesions spare semantic knowledge while disrupting the flexible organisation of behaviour it supports <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Duncan et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Shallice, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Shallice and Burgess, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Hassan may know that smoking causes cancer and yet make no effort to quit until his PFC embeds this relational knowledge into representations of his daily routine.
The PFC could learn this structure from other circuits that encode abstract cognitive maps, in temporal (Section 4.4) and parietal (Bottini and Doeller, 2020) areas.

text.text: It is an intriguing prospect that we can now move towards an integrated mechanistic understanding of how different cognitive maps interact to enable flexible behaviour.
By combining precise theories with emerging experimental tools, our field is poised for a revolution in its mechanistic understanding of cognitive functions.

Actions Volitional choices about states the animal can plan over.
These can be low level actions, like moving a particular limb.
They can also be more abstract actions, like choosing to pursue a degree.
This definition of actions treats the firing of PFC neurons for e.g. spatial locations as encoding the decision to move to such location.
Any variable that determines which action is appropriate in a given situation -including task rules, ordinal position within a sequence, preference rank, or the identity of an agent.
In DSRs, context is encoded conjunctively with action -the same action is represented by different neurons depending on its context.
The statistical regularities governing how actions relate to one another.
This includes the periodicities by which actions repeat and how frequently certain action transitions occur.

In the DSR framework, action statistics are embedded in the synaptic connectivity between duplicated action representations, allowing the network to favour more probable action combinations and suppress improbable ones.
Network activity that evolves towards stable representations known as 'attractor states'.
The stability of different representations is determined by the pattern of synaptic connections.
In DSRs, structured connectivity between action representations gives rise to attractor states that encode more probable action combinations.
This allows planning and inference to emerge from dynamic relaxation rather than sequential search.
A representational strategy in which different task variables, such as abstract context and concrete actions, are encoded by separate neural populations and combined only at decision time.
This is in contrast to DSRs, where context and action are encoded conjunctively by the same neurons.
A phenomenon where neurons respond to conjunctions of multiple task variables, such as an action and its context, rather than a single variable in isolation.
The process by which downstream circuits extract information from a neural population.
DSRs represent action combinations in static population activity patterns, which allows a linear readout mechanism to decode the relevant information without needing to integrate activity over time.
A low-dimensional subset of the high-dimensional space of all possible population activity patterns.
In DSRs, different copies of the same action are represented in non-overlapping subspaces, each dedicated to a given context.
This allows simultaneous encoding of multiple action-context combinations in population activity.
A framework in which the PFC learns the abstract statistical structure of a class of tasks through slow synaptic plasticity across many experiences.
Once this structure is embedded in connectivity, the PFC can rapidly adapt to new tasks of the same class through fast recurrent dynamics alone, without further synaptic changes.
DSRs can embed two classes of structured connectivity.
The first is 'persistent' connectivity, which is always active and determines the stable activity patterns, or "fixed points", of a neural network.
The second is 'gated' connectivity, which is activated by additional context signals to move neural activity between fixed points.
This connectivity between duplicated representations reflects ubiquitous action statistics.
For example, a representation of 'sowing' in the morning might excite a representation of 'watering' in the afternoon and inhibit representations of 'harvesting' in the near future.

This idea has close parallels in visual cortex, where neurons with distant receptive fields are more frequently connected if they have similar orientation selectivity (Iacaruso et al., 2017) (Figure a: Persistent connectivity in visual cortex reflects the prevalence of straight lines in natural environments).

text.text: We will see that PFC uses the same principle to infer representations of future actions, which enables efficient planning.
This connectivity implements structured operations over neural representations, such as swapping two sequence elements.
Like persistent connectivity, gated connectivity reflects action statistics.
Unlike persistent connectivity, gated connections are selectively engaged by additional context signals.
Gated connections are well known from Drosophila, where a single head direction (HD) cell preferentially excites its 'clockwise' (CW) neighbor when the fly is turning clockwise and vice versa.
This control of effective connectivity is achieved by two auxiliary 'turn' populations that implement the CW and CCW operations.

When (de)activating the turn populations, HD cells change their effective connectivity to implement the appropriate rotation (Figure c: Gated 'left' and 'right' connections in the fruit fly head direction circuit implement angular velocity integration).
PFC similarly controls the effective connectivity between duplicated representations by gating auxiliary neural populations that implement abstract computations.

Such gating can be implemented through neurons that are conjunctively tuned to an operation and its substrate, similar to conjunctive cells that update spatial representations (Sargolini et al., 2006; Turner-Evans et al., 2017 , 2020).

(2026) found initial representations of the 'first presented' and 'second presented' item in orthogonal subspaces of macaque lateral PFC (left).

After the values of both items were known, the representation of 'chosen item' became aligned across trials irrespective of its order of presentation (right). (f)Knudsen and Wallis (2020)  recorded value representations that were ranked by preference in macaque OFC (top).
This is consistent with recent models of DSRs for rewardguided behaviours(Warren et al., 2026; bottom).

text.text: Figure 6: DSRs across the prefrontal cortex. (a) Evolution has grown the human PFC to almost 3 billion neurons.
However, the models discussed in this review only use tens to hundreds of neurons.

This is partly because we have considered small state spaces, but it is also because we have ignored much of the heterogeneity in PFC. (b) DSRs for sensorimotor computations have been discovered in dorsolateral PFC (top; Xie et al. 2022), while DSRs for allocentric locations have been discovered in medial PFC (bottom; El-Gaby et al.
This mirrors the distinct afferents from parietal cortex to dorsolateral PFC and from the hippocampal formation to medial PFC.

Both types of DSRs require gated 'conveyor belt' connections to read out sequences, but they operate on different action modalities and embed structure related to each modality's action statistics. (c) Neurons represent increasingly more abstract actions from posterior to anterior PFC (left).
If such hierarchical representations are combined with DSRs, it enables hierarchical planning (right).
This mitigates the challenge of computing long sequences in DSRs. (d) Separate PFC representations have been recorded for self and other.
If these representations are embedded in DSRs, it could enable social computations.
In this case, Hassan knows that his daughter is more likely to help with the harvest tomorrow if she has a big breakfast.
He therefore infers that he should buy eggs this evening to have the ingredients for pancakes in the morning.
Factorised codes for context and action can also be encoded by individual neurons or by population patterns (Figure a).
In the neuron doctrine case, individual neurons encode different contexts.
In the population doctrine, context is encoded by a linear combination of neurons.
